rationale: Clinical delineation of GTPBP2-related Jaberi-Elahi syndrome demonstrates that ectodermal findings (sparse hair, dental anomalies, dysplastic nails) and brain iron accumulation are age-dependent and evolve over time, presenting most prominently in older children and adults. In neonates and young infants, initial manifestations are dominated by severe congenital microcephaly, profound hypotonia, and early neurodevelopmental delay, whereas overt ectodermal dysplasias may be absent or unexpressed. Consequently, ectodermal abnormalities cannot serve as mandatory criteria for differentiating affected infants under 12 months of age from clinical mimics such as infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy (PLAN) or pontocerebellar hypoplasias.

evidence.text: Carter et al. delineate the clinical trajectory of GTPBP2 deficiency and observe that ectodermal manifestations and peripheral neuropathy are age-related and most prominent in older individuals, while early presentations center on prenatal microcephaly and tone abnormalities.

source.title: Clinical delineation of GTPBP2‐associated neuro‐ectodermal syndrome: Report of two new families and review of the literature
source.quote: Our findings suggest that some aspects of the clinical presentation appear to be age-related; brain iron accumulation may appear only after childhood, and the ectodermal findings and peripheral neuropathy are most prominent in older individuals.

evidence.text: A comprehensive literature review of 28 individuals with Jaberi-Elahi syndrome identified sparse hair in 26 of 28 patients (92.9%), demonstrating that ectodermal hair changes are not universally detected across all assessed patients.

source.title: Jaberi-Elahi syndrome: Exploring a novel GTPBP2 mutation and a literature review
source.quote: A large numbers of patients manifest motor development delay (26/28), sparse hair (26/28), and speech disorder (24/28). Moreover, a significant fraction of patients suffer from intellectual disability (23/28), hypotonia (23/28), skeletal problems (23/28), and visual impairment (18/28).

evidence.text: Soğukpınar et al. describe an infant presenting with congenital neurodevelopmental abnormalities and highlight that GTPBP2-related disease must be considered in young infants even prior to the classic full phenotypic spectrum.

new_directions.question_text: What is the median age of onset for each specific ectodermal feature (hypotrichosis, oligodontia/hypodontia, nail dystrophy) in confirmed GTPBP2 deficiency?
new_directions.rationale: Quantifying the exact chronological emergence of dental, hair, and ungual signs would define the precise clinical window during which phenotypic overlap with purely neurological phenocopies is highest.

new_directions.question_text: Can high-resolution neuroimaging findings (e.g., specific cerebellar folial atrophy or pontine volume loss patterns) reliably distinguish infant-stage Jaberi-Elahi syndrome from PLA2G6-associated neuroaxonal dystrophy before iron accumulation appears?
new_directions.rationale: Because both disorders can show progressive cerebellar atrophy and delay in early infancy prior to iron deposition or ectodermal manifestations, systematic comparison of early MRI metrics would provide immediate diagnostic utility.
